newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU set to tighten human rights pressure on Burma.
newsitem.headline: EU set to tighten human rights pressure on Burma.

text.p: The European Union, angry at a lack of progress on human rights and democracy in Burma, is set to increase pressure on Rangoon on Monday by imposing tight restrictions on visas and high-level contacts.

EU diplomats said top officials from the 15-nation bloc had agreed new steps against Burma's ruling State Law and Order Restoration Council (SLORC) following what the EU sees as an unwillingness by the regime to improve its record.
The steps were to be rubber stamped by EU foreign ministers at a meeting in Luxembourg on Monday.
"The situation in Burma has deteriorated," one diplomat said. "A number of EU states have indicated the need for a strong signal."
Burma's military government has triggered international protests by detaining a top official in Nobel Peace laureate's Aung San Suu Kyi's National League for Democracy (NLD) party.
Diplomats in Burma said the official, Kyi Maung, was detained for questioning on Wednesday after being seen speaking to two students before a rare sit-in protest.

Actions to be agreed by the EU foreign ministers include banning entry visas for members of the SLORC and their families and for top members of the military or security forces viewed as impeding democracy in the Southeast Asian nation.
EU ministers and other bloc officials will also be banned from visiting Burma for bilateral meetings.
In addition, the EU agreement renews for six months existing sanctions against Burma, which include a suspension of non-humanitarian aid or development programmes.

The EU has been slowly turning up the heat on the SLORC since summer when Denmark began lobbying for action following the death in prison in Burma of James Leander Nichols, its unaccredited honorary consul.
Nichols, who also represented EU member Finland and non-members Norway and Switzerland, was Suu Kyi's godfather.

Denmark and some of the other Nordic countries would like the EU to take stronger action, including perhaps economic sanctions, but most countries argues that the EU could not act without the United Nations.

Diplomats said that recent failures to get a positive response from the SLORC on democracy and human rights had spurred the latest EU move, which also includes a warning that further measures may be considered.

Irish Foreign Minister Dick Spring, representing the EU presidency, had what diplomats said was a fruitless meeting with Burmese Foreign Minister Ohn Gyaw in September on the margin of the U.N. general assembly.
"There was no flexibility at all on the Burmese side," one diplomat said.
The United States has also recently barred SLORC members from getting U.S. visas.
